title: The vow
hookLine: a promise said out loud in front of people; Shantideva takes the vow, and the poem comes full circle
tomorrow: the vow is made. what keeps it from slipping?

cards: There's a reason people make big promises in front of other people. Graduation pledges. Wedding vows.
A new citizen with one hand raised. You could promise the same thing alone in your room, but it isn't quite the same. Said out loud, in front of witnesses, a promise starts to hold you.
So, yesterday's question: jewel in hand, what does Shantideva promise next? He makes the vow, and he makes it in front of everyone.

teach.h: AS THE BUDDHAS BEFORE ME DID.
teach.b: Chapter three's heart is the bodhisattva vow.

Shantideva says: just as the Buddhas of the past took up the awakening mind and trained in it step by step, so I too, for the good of the world, take it up and will train in it step by step. He isn't inventing a promise.
He's stepping into one others have made. Then the line that closes the circle from two weeks ago.
Remember hard to find, the blind turtle and this rare human life? Now he says: today my life is fruitful. This human life was well gained.
Today I'm born into the Buddha's family.

teach.h: IN FRONT OF ALL THE PROTECTORS.
teach.b: And at the chapter's end, in front of all the protectors, he invites the whole world to awakening, and until then, to happiness. The witnesses matter. So does the word today.
Not someday, after more practice. The rare life from the first week gets its point in this one.

how: In Mahayana Buddhism the bodhisattva vow is often taken in a ceremony before a teacher and images of the Buddhas, and some practitioners recite verses from this chapter daily to renew it.

games.q: the vow and the two weeks — tap the pairs.
p: took it up and trained step by step
the rare human life, put to use

s: Shantideva writes a brand-new vow of his own invention
he steps into the promise the Buddhas of the past made, and trains step by step as they did.
after the vow he says today his life is fruitful
this human life, he says, was well gained; today he's born into the Buddha's family.
the vow only counts once you're far along the path
he says today, not someday: the rare life gets its point now.

games.q: you want to promise your little sister you'll help with her reading. what fits Shantideva's vow?
o: promise to help her every single day, forever, so it sounds big enough.
make a specific promise you can keep, say it to her, and start this week.
don't promise anything, in case life gets busy and you let her down.
games.why: Shantideva's vow is said before witnesses and kept step by step. a real, specific promise, said out loud and begun, is the shape of it.

practice: Sit up, hands resting together. Think of one person or group whose good you care about, and find one promise for them you can actually keep, small and specific.
Say it out loud, quietly, once, as if someone you respect were listening. Then sit with it.

wordCard.voice: The vow: Shantideva taking up the awakening mind for the good of the world, as the Buddhas before him did, in front of witnesses.

orig.note: Sanskrit: restraint, a vow. The bodhisattva vow is often called the bodhisattva samvara.

carryVoice: Your line: today my life is fruitful. Hard to find, and now put to use. Three chapters read; two weeks done.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 3.22-3.26 (as the Buddhas of the past took up the awakening mind, so do I; today my life is fruitful; born into the Buddha's family)
Bodhicaryavatara 3.33 (before all the protectors, inviting the world to awakening and, meanwhile, to happiness)
